entries.name: Partial Information Decomposition
entries.senseHere: A mathematical framework that splits the information two or more sources carry about a target into separate pieces: information they share redundantly, information each carries uniquely, and information that only appears when their patterns are combined (synergy).
entries.background: Introduced by Williams and Beer as an extension of classical information theory to handle multiple interacting sources, it has since been applied across neuroscience, climate science, and sociology.

entries.name: rich club
entries.senseHere: The subset of best-connected neurons in a network that are more densely interconnected with each other than chance would predict, found here to concentrate most of the network's synergistic computation.

entries.name: mutual information
entries.senseHere: A measure of how much knowing the state of one variable reduces uncertainty about another; used here as a stand-in for undirected statistical dependence between neurons, akin to a nonlinear correlation.

entries.name: transfer entropy
entries.senseHere: A directional measure of how much a neuron's past activity reduces uncertainty about another neuron's future activity, beyond what that second neuron's own past already explains; used as a proxy for information flow or effective connectivity between neurons.

entries.name: functional connectivity
entries.senseHere: An undirected measure of statistical similarity between two neurons' activity patterns, without implying that one caused or transmitted information to the other; captured here using mutual information.

entries.name: effective connectivity
entries.senseHere: A directed, time-ordered measure of how one neuron's activity actually influences another's future activity, as opposed to mere co-occurrence; captured here using transfer entropy.

entries.name: synergy
entries.senseHere: Information about a target neuron's future that can only be learned by observing two or more source neurons together, not from any one alone, treated here as a signature of genuine neural computation.

entries.name: redundancy
entries.senseHere: Information about a target that could be learned equally well from any one of several sources on its own, so it gets 'double counted' if their individual contributions are simply added up.

entries.name: unique information
entries.senseHere: The portion of information about a target that only one particular source discloses, which no other source in the group can provide.

entries.name: redundancy function
entries.senseHere: A chosen rule for quantifying exactly how much information counts as 'redundant' among a set of sources; this choice is not fixed by classical information theory and determines the rest of the PID decomposition.

entries.name: Imin
entries.senseHere: The original, simplest redundancy function proposed for PID, widely used in the neural studies discussed but criticized for producing unintuitive results in some cases.

entries.name: computational triad
entries.senseHere: The basic unit of analysis in this work: two source neurons that both send signals to one shared target neuron, on which a three-variable PID is performed.

entries.name: partial information lattice
entries.senseHere: A structured diagram listing every distinct way that a set of source variables can share information about a target, ordered so that simpler combinations sit below more complex ones; PID values are computed by moving through this structure.

entries.name: organotypic cultures
entries.senseHere: Thin slices of mouse brain tissue grown in nutrient media that preserve much of the original circuit wiring, used here as the living neural networks recorded for PID analysis.

entries.name: recurrent connections
entries.senseHere: Within a computational triad, direct links between the two source neurons themselves, found to be associated with higher synergy.

entries.name: feedforward connections
entries.senseHere: Within a computational triad, the links running from the two source neurons to the shared target neuron; both must be present for a triad to exist.

entries.name: feedback connections
entries.senseHere: Within a computational triad, links running from the target neuron back to one or both of its source neurons.

entries.name: Dedekind number
entries.senseHere: A rapidly growing sequence of numbers that gives the count of distinct information-sharing modes (PI atoms) for a given number of source variables, explaining why PID becomes impractical for many sources.
entries.background: Dedekind numbers count a specific class of logical structures called monotone Boolean functions, and only the first nine terms of the sequence are currently known.

entries.name: O-information
entries.senseHere: A scalable heuristic measure of overall redundancy versus synergy across a whole system, used as a practical substitute for full PID when the number of variables makes the exact decomposition computationally impossible.

entries.name: local PID
entries.senseHere: A version of partial information decomposition applied to single, specific moments or configurations of activity rather than to overall averages, allowing a moment-by-moment time series of redundancy and synergy to be built.

entries.name: integrated information decomposition
entries.senseHere: An extension of PID that decomposes information shared between groups of variables across two time points or across multiple targets, rather than just one target at one moment.
